topic: sub:12|Relative frequency and probability|Probability of equally likely outcomes

parts.latex:
Lachlan buys 8 tickets in a raffle where 240 tickets were sold. He wins first prize.

What is the probability that he wins the second prize given that Lachlan has already won first prize?

solutions.latex:
After Lachlan wins first prize, there are $239$ tickets left, and $7$ of them are his.
$$P(\text{wins 2nd prize}) = \dfrac{7}{239}$$

6133.stem:
The wheel below is spun around until it stops on a number. The wheel is equally likely to stop on any number.

\exfigure{720_q5_1}

parts.latex: What is the probability the wheel stops on 3?
Find the probability the wheel stops on a number less than 10.
Find the probability the wheel stops on a number divisible by 4.

solutions.latex:
There are 12 equally likely outcomes, and one of them is 3.
$$P(3) = \dfrac{1}{12}$$

The numbers less than 10 are $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(<10) &= \dfrac{9}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{4} \end{aligned}$$

The numbers divisible by 4 are $4, 8, 12$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{divisible by } 4) &= \dfrac{3}{12} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4} \end{aligned}$$

720_q5_1.notes: Spinner with 12 exactly equal 30° sectors, since the question says it is equally likely to stop on any number. The crop's sector lines are a little uneven, so a few lines differ by a few px; that accounts for the red/blue in the overlay. Numbers are in the same order and positions. The red hub is drawn light grey with the spokes showing (rule 6, black and white only).

parts.latex: The probability of a team winning a particular football match is $\dfrac{3}{7}$, and the probability of drawing this match is $\dfrac{1}{5}$. The probability of this team winning or drawing the match would be closest to:

solutions.latex:
Winning and drawing are mutually exclusive, so the probabilities add.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{win or draw}) &= \dfrac{3}{7} + \dfrac{1}{5} \\ &= \dfrac{22}{35} \\ &\approx 0.63 \end{aligned}$$
So the correct option is A.

6295.stem:
In a game, an unbiased die with the numbers 1 to 6 is rolled twice.

The product of the two uppermost numbers on the die represents the player's score in the game.

figures.cap: blank 6 by 6 product table, 1st roll and 2nd roll

parts.latex:
Fill in the table below to show the sample space for this game.

\exfigure{718_q11_1}
What is the probability that the highest score will be thrown?
What is the probability of the score being a multiple of 5?

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source already has the completed table drawing.

solutions.latex:
The highest score is $6\times 6=36$, which occurs once in the 36 equally likely outcomes.
$$P(36)=\dfrac{1}{36}$$

The scores that are multiples of 5 come from a 5 on either roll: 11 outcomes out of 36.
$$P(\text{multiple of }5)=\dfrac{11}{36}$$

718_q11_1.notes: Blank 6×6 product table transcribed (rule 8). The '1st roll' header spans the six columns and the rotated '2nd roll' label spans the six body rows. The two empty top-left cells have no border on the paper.

718_q11_s1.notes: Completed product table transcribed (rule 8). Same layout and spans as 718_q11_1; the handwritten green products are typeset.

solutions.latex:
The score is a 2-digit number, tens digit from the first wheel and units digit from the second wheel. Each wheel has equal sectors.

Score at least 40: the tens digit must be 4 or 5, so
$$P(\text{tens digit} \ge 4) = \dfrac{2}{5}$$

Score even: the units digit must be even. The second wheel has two even numbers (4 and 2) out of 4 sectors, so
$$P(\text{even units digit}) = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

The two spins are independent, so
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{even and at least } 40) &= \dfrac{2}{5}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{option B}$$

meta.self_check: The key B (1/5) needs exactly two even numbers on the second wheel. The printed digit in the bottom-left sector of the second wheel is ambiguous (reads like 6 or 9) and is taken as 9 to match the key.

parts.latex:
Jack was rolling an unbiased die. He rolled a 5 followed by a 2.

How would you describe the probability of Jack rolling an even number on the next roll of the die?

solutions.latex:
The die is unbiased, so each roll is independent of the previous rolls.

The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so
$$P(\text{even})=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$
A probability of $\dfrac{1}{2}$ is an even chance, not likely, unlikely or certain.

$$\therefore\ \text{the probability is described as even}$$

parts.latex:
There are five more black marbles in a bag than there are white marbles.

All marbles in the bag are either black or white.

The probability of randomly selecting a black marble from the bag is $\dfrac{3}{5}$.

How many white marbles are in the bag?

solutions.latex:
Let there be $x$ white marbles, so there are $x+5$ black marbles and $2x+5$ in total.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{x+5}{2x+5} &= \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 5x+25 &= 6x+15 \\ x &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
So the answer is A.

7163.stem: Twenty cards are numbered from 1 to 20.

parts.latex: Find the probability that the card drawn is an odd number.
Find the probability the card is divisible by both 2 and 3.

solutions.latex:
There are 10 odd numbers among the 20 cards.
$$P(\text{odd}) = \dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2} \text{ (or } 50\% \text{ or } 0.5)$$

Divisible by both 2 and 3 means divisible by 6: the cards 6, 12, 18.
$$P(\text{both 2 and 3}) = \dfrac{3}{20} \text{ (or } 0.15 \text{ or } 15\% \text{)}$$

parts.latex:
There are five more black marbles in a bag than there are white marbles.

All marbles in the bag are either black or white.

The probability of randomly selecting a black marble from the bag is $\dfrac{3}{5}$.

How many white marbles are in the bag?

solutions.latex:
Let $w$ be the number of white marbles, so there are $w+5$ black marbles and $2w+5$ marbles in total.

The probability of a black marble is $\dfrac{3}{5}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{w+5}{2w+5} &= \dfrac{3}{5} \\ 5w+25 &= 6w+15 \\ w &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $15$ black out of $25$ marbles gives $\dfrac{15}{25}=\dfrac{3}{5}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{there are 10 white marbles (option A)}$$

The number of students with at least two siblings is $3+1+1=5$, out of $5+10+3+1+1=20$ students.

$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least } 2) &= \dfrac{3+1+1}{5+10+3+1+1} \\ &= \dfrac{5}{20} \\ &= 0.25 \end{aligned}$$

Hence the answer is D.
